summary: Describes the environment and goals for using the IEEE 802.15.4e Time-Slotted Channel Hopping MAC in low-power and lossy networks. It lists an initial set of problems that IETF work must address to run IP over such networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny wireless sensors take turns talking and hop between radio channels to avoid noise. This explains the problems to solve to make that work with internet rules.

subtitle: Planning for time-slotted wireless networks in the Internet of Things

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4e defines TSCH, a medium access control (MAC) protocol for low-power wireless networks that uses synchronized time slots and channel hopping to achieve reliability and efficiency. However, the standard defines only the mechanisms; it does not specify how to build and maintain the communication schedule that controls which nodes transmit when.
tldr.mechanism: This document outlines the problems that must be solved to integrate TSCH with IPv6 routing and application protocols. It identifies requirements for network formation, resource management, scheduling, security, and timing that must be addressed by a higher-layer entity called the Logical Link Control (LLC).
tldr.outcome: The document serves as a foundation for the IETF 6TiSCH working group, which is developing standards (such as the 6top sublayer) to provide the LLC functionality missing from the TSCH standard and to let IPv6-based IoT networks run reliably over TSCH.

today: RFC 7554 remains the foundational problem statement for TSCH-based IoT. The 6TiSCH working group has developed standards to address these problems, including the 6top (6TiSCH Operation Sublayer) protocols and 6TiSCH minimal configuration specifications. Deployments using TSCH are now active, especially in industrial and building automation contexts.

sections.title: TSCH and Low-Power Wireless Networks
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.15.4e standard amended the popular IEEE 802.15.4 wireless standard with a new medium access control (MAC) mode called TSCH (Time-Slotted Channel Hopping). TSCH is designed for low-power, lossy networks (LLNs) where battery-powered devices need to operate reliably in harsh radio environments with interference and fading.

Unlike traditional WiFi or cellular networks that use contention (devices listen and transmit when the channel seems free), TSCH divides time into synchronized slots and assigns each slot to a specific pair of nodes on a specific radio frequency. This time synchronization and channel hopping approach dramatically reduces power consumption (nodes can sleep most of the time) and improves reliability (interference on one frequency does not block all communication).

TSCH is the foundation for IPv6 over TSCH networks, as described in the 6TiSCH working group. However, TSCH itself defines only the MAC mechanisms; it does not define how to build, maintain, and adapt the communication schedule as the network changes.
sections.plainLanguage: TSCH is a wireless method where devices take turns talking at scheduled times and switch frequencies automatically. It saves power and works well even in noisy places.

sections.title: TSCH Core Concepts
sections.content:
In a TSCH network, time is organized into time slots (typically 10 milliseconds). Slots are grouped into slotframes that repeat continuously. Each device maintains a schedule (a table that specifies, for each slot and frequency pair, whether to transmit, receive, or sleep). The schedule is referenced by absolute slot number (ASN), a counter that increments with each slot across the entire network lifetime.

Channel hopping means that even though the schedule is fixed, the actual frequency used changes automatically: frequency = function((ASN + offset) mod number_of_channels). This ensures that a fixed schedule hops across all available frequencies over time, so interference on any single channel does not break communication.

Cells are the atomic scheduling units. A dedicated cell is reserved for one specific pair of nodes; a shared cell allows multiple nodes to contend using a slotted Aloha mechanism. Bundles are collections of cells between the same pair of nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Time slots are 10 ms windows. A schedule repeats and tells each device what to do: send, listen, or sleep. Frequencies change automatically so static schedules hop across the band.

sections.title: Scheduling Problems That Must Be Solved
sections.content:
A Logical Link Control (LLC) entity must solve several scheduling and network management problems that TSCH leaves unanswered:

Network formation and joining: How do new devices discover the network, synchronize to the TSCH schedule, and get assigned cells? How is the join process secured?

Multi-hop topology: TSCH schedules packets between neighboring nodes, but IPv6 routes span many hops. The LLC must ensure cells exist along the routes that the IPv6 routing protocol (RPL) establishes.

Resource management: How many cells should be allocated between two neighbors based on traffic? How do neighbors negotiate adding or removing cells as traffic changes?

Scheduling mechanisms: Should cells be assigned by a central scheduler, computed locally by pairs of neighbors, or a mix of both? Different mechanisms may suit different applications.

Security: TSCH provides mechanisms to encrypt frames given a key, but does not define how to generate keys or bootstrap security for joining nodes.

Timing and synchronization: All nodes must maintain tight clock synchronization. The LLC must assign each node a time-source neighbor and prevent synchronization loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone must decide: how nodes join, where cells go for multi-hop routes, how many cells each link gets, who assigns cells, and how to keep clocks synchronized and secure.

sections.title: TSCH Architecture and IPv6 Integration
sections.content:
TSCH sits at the MAC layer, below 6LoWPAN (which adapts IPv6 to fit in small wireless frames) and RPL (which handles IPv6 routing in low-power, lossy networks). The LLC is a new functional layer between TSCH and the higher protocol stack.

RPL builds a directed acyclic graph of routes to a central collection point (the root). Once RPL routes are known, the LLC can allocate TSCH cells to carry traffic along those routes. RPL needs to know the network topology; the LLC can gather that information by monitoring link quality and feeding it to RPL.

Different deployment scenarios may use different scheduling strategies. An industrial application with predictable traffic might use a centralized scheduler (a Path Computation Element) to optimize the schedule. A home sensor network might use a distributed, adaptive algorithm where neighbors negotiate cells as needed. The LLC must support these different approaches, or at least not prevent them.
sections.plainLanguage: TSCH is at the wireless level. Above it sits a new scheduler (LLC) that feeds routes to TSCH cells and tells RPL what links are available.

sections.title: Reliability and Deterministic Behavior
sections.content:
A key advantage of TSCH's scheduled approach is that it enables deterministic communication. Unlike random-access networks where a packet may experience variable delays or loss due to contention, a TSCH network with a well-built schedule guarantees that a packet will be delivered by a known deadline if the link is working.

The LLC must ensure that cells are allocated so that packets carrying time-sensitive data (e.g., industrial control) reach their destination before a deadline. Simultaneously, the LLC must support bursty or lower-priority traffic that does not have strict timing requirements. This means the scheduling entity must balance guaranteed delivery for some flows with best-effort delivery for others.

Link quality varies over time. The LLC must be able to adapt the schedule—adding cells to paths that are congested or losing reliability, removing cells from unused links—to maintain both determinism for priority traffic and overall network health.
sections.plainLanguage: With the right schedule, packets arrive on time every time. But the scheduler must balance strict deadlines for important data with flexible timing for everyday traffic.
